findings.statement: Obligation 1 (atomically bind one spawned agent_id to one run, assignment, and digest) is DISCHARGED on the current bytes. Run: the Start-time lease is the sole run resolver and the ACTIVE_RUN fallback is gone (subagent_stop_validate.py:138-160), so a leaseless agent inside an active run is blocked. Assignment: the parent-minted receipt at .agent-harness/admissions/<run>/<assignment>.json is compared with hmac.compare_digest(token_digest(proof), receipt.token_digest) (line 238). Digest: the receipt's assignment_sha256 and the lease's sealed digest are both checked against a single read of the assignment bytes (lines 165-190, 225-230), so the parsed contract and the attributed digest describe the same bytes. agent_id: receipt.expected_agent_id is enforced at line 244-250 and admit_agent.py:117-125 makes --expect-agent-id mandatory unless the explicit --agent-id-unknown opt-out is passed; all three r4 mint rows carry expected_agent_id. Atomicity of consumption rests on the O_EXCL claim (line 385), not on the earlier state read, and the four-process concurrency fixture asserts exactly one attribution row. Three bounding caveats that do not change the verdict: (a) --agent-id-unknown still permits a token-only receipt, so a leaked token would then admit any agent; (b) the MINT is not atomic against a concurrent mint for the same assignment (target.exists() then write, no O_EXCL) -- probe P5 measured one winner and three refusals across four concurrent mints, but that is process-startup timing, not a guarantee, and the failure mode is fail-closed (last receipt wins, the loser's agent blocks); (c) under the recorded LOCAL-ADAPT the whole Stop event JSON including agent_id is authored by the parent, so the binding is enforced against a parent-declared identifier rather than a runtime-attested one.
assumptions_used: SubagentStart never receives the spawn prompt (frozen rows D-031/D-032), so a parent-minted binding is the only available mechanism.
The stated same-OS-user forgery residual is out of scope per the assignment brief.

findings.statement: Obligation 2 (make receipt/lease creation failure a hard Start failure) is only HALF DISCHARGED. The LEASE half is fully met: subagent_start_context.py:143-155 no longer swallows the OSError -- it emits `Run lease: NOT RECORDED (<Error>)`, appends a start_error, renders `Hook preflight: FAIL`, and sets the systemMessage warning, and SubagentStop then blocks the leaseless agent. This is fixture-covered (test_subagentstart_hard_fails_when_lease_cannot_be_written), mutation-verified (swallowing the OSError kills exactly that test), and live-attested on committed bytes by the C3 canary (raw_logs/start_out_d067-canary-c3-leasefail.json shows `Run lease: NOT RECORDED (PermissionError)` and `Hook preflight: FAIL`; stop_out shows the block). The RECEIPT half is NOT met: SubagentStart contains no reference to .agent-harness/admissions/ at all. Probe P1 measured this directly -- with zero receipts minted anywhere in the active run, SubagentStart emits `Hook preflight: PASS - canonical context and runtime identity verified` and systemMessage null. A receipt-creation failure is therefore a parent-side admit_agent.py exit-1 plus a hard *Stop* failure, never a hard Start failure. The security property is preserved (the agent cannot produce an admissible result), so this is fail-closed, not fail-open; but the obligation as D-065 wrote it is not satisfied, and the practical cost is that an agent spawned without a receipt performs an entire session before discovering at Stop that it cannot submit. The check is feasible at Start: receipts carry expected_agent_id and SubagentStart knows agent_id, so Start could require an `open` receipt naming this agent in the active run. Separately, probe P2 shows the true receipt-write failure at mint (admissions dir unwritable) exits 1 with no receipt but leaves an orphan `minted` ledger row that validate_harness does not reconcile; harmless and fail-closed, but it is evidence noise in an append-only ledger.
assumptions_used: "Hard Start failure" is read as D-065 wrote it: the failure must surface at SubagentStart, not only at SubagentStop.
reproduction: grep -n 'admission' .codex/hooks/subagent_start_context.py  # no match

findings.statement: Obligation 3 (add same-run substitution and receipt-write-failure negative fixtures) is DISCHARGED, with one named coverage gap that does not overturn it. Both fixtures exist and neither is vacuous. (1) test_hooks.py:730 test_subagentstop_blocks_same_run_assignment_substitution reproduces the D-065 controlled negative faithfully: the Start-time lease seals BOTH assignments (write_lease(..., assignment_ids=(ASSIGNMENT_ID, other_id))), so every D-058 check passes and only the parent-minted token distinguishes them; it asserts the specific block reason 'admission_proof does not match', which is emitted only at subagent_stop_validate.py:238-243, and it asserts both receipts remain `open`. Mutation-proven non-vacuous: replacing that one guard with `if False:` fails exactly this test and leaves the other 38 passing. It is additionally live-attested on committed bytes by the C2 canary block. (2) test_hooks.py:1104 test_admit_agent_fails_closed_when_ledger_cannot_be_written carries the docstring 'Receipt-write-failure fixture: no receipt may outlive a failed mint' and is mutation-proven load-bearing for the ledger-before-receipt ordering. GAP: it chmods the RUN directory, so what actually fails is the ADMISSIONS.jsonl append, not the receipt write; the genuine receipt-write path (dump_json_atomic(target, receipt) raising) has no committed fixture. I exercised that path manually (probe P2) and confirmed it is fail-closed. So the obligation's named fixture exists and is real, but its name overstates its coverage by one path. I also ran a deliberate vacuity sweep against the whole D-067 fixture set for the `str(x or y) != y` failure class named in my brief: six independent single-guard mutations (token comparison, expected_agent_id enforcement, admit_agent mint ordering, SubagentStart lease-error swallow, stop-hook consume ordering, planted-claim attribution guard, validate_harness reverse ledger reconciliation) each killed exactly one test and left the remaining 38 green. No vacuously-passing guard was found in the D-067 fixtures.
assumptions_used: A fixture is non-vacuous if reverting the single guard it names causes it, and only it, to fail.

findings.statement: Obligation 4 (pass a replacement live overlapping-run canary with unique write attribution) is NOT DISCHARGED ON THE CURRENT BYTES, because the canary predates them. The C1/C2/C3 canaries ran at 2026-07-29T02:37-02:41Z (11:37-11:41 JST). .codex/hooks/subagent_stop_validate.py was then modified by commit 96089f0 at 13:10 JST, +29/-12 lines, and the change lands precisely inside the acceptance path the canary exercises: the ledger-before-receipt consume ordering, the claim release on consume failure, and the installed_here bypass fix. No live canary has been re-run since. The only ledger rows anywhere post-96089f0 are the three `minted` rows in run-20260729-f10-d067-review-r4; there is not a single post-96089f0 `consumed` row in the repository, so no live acceptance has ever been observed on the bytes now under judgement. Compounding this, 96089f0's own commit message records that the preceding round-3 fix commit 07e3507 staged an explicit path list omitting .codex/hooks, so the two stop-hook fixes the audit document describes as landed were in fact left in the working tree -- committed bytes did not match reviewed bytes at the moment the audit document was written. That is now reconciled, but it is the same defect class this review was told to weigh. Two further evidentiary limits on the existing canary: (a) the OVERLAP is corroborated but not attested -- init_run.py writes ACTIVE_RUN, and the decoy RUN_PLAN.json records created_at 2026-07-29T02:40:10+00:00, the same second as the C1 consume row, but same-second equality cannot establish ordering and no committed artifact records ACTIVE_RUN's value at C1's stop; (b) the retained C1 stop event was scrubbed, so its admission_proof now holds the token digest rather than the token, making the artifact non-replayable, and acceptance is attested by a zero-byte stop_out (an absence) plus the ledger row. What IS solidly established is the write attribution itself: I recomputed both canary result digests and they match their ledger rows byte-for-byte (C1 sha256:0e7b3cac..., C2 sha256:7e576e51...), each row naming a distinct agent_id. So attribution is unique and verifiable; the LIVE overlapping-run canary against current bytes is simply absent.
assumptions_used: A live canary attests only the bytes it executed against; a subsequent edit to the acceptance path invalidates it as evidence for the new bytes.
Ledger timestamps are UTC and commit dates are +0900, so 02:40Z precedes the 13:10 JST commit by ~1.5 hours.

findings.statement: Cross-cutting: the append-only admission ledger does NOT permanently pin admitted bytes, because validate_harness.py reconciles last-row-wins. validate_harness.py:223 assigns ledger_consumed[assignment_id] = row inside the scan loop, so a second `consumed` row for the same assignment silently supersedes the first, and the post-hoc-edit detector is cleared. Two reachable routes, neither requiring the stated same-OS-user forgery residual. Route A (sanctioned, probe P4b): accept a result, edit the artifact (validate_harness correctly reports ok:false, 'Result artifact differs from the bytes recorded in the admission ledger'), then run the documented `admit_agent.py --reopen --reason ...` and re-stop -- a second consume row is appended and validate_harness reports ok:true with the edit laundered. admit_agent.py's own --reopen help text concedes exactly this ('until the reopened assignment is consumed again'), and test_reopen_cannot_clear_the_tamper_detector asserts only the intermediate state (reopened, not yet re-consumed), stopping one step short of the state that clears the detector. Route B (probe P4a): delete only the gitignored <receipt>.json.claim file; the same agent then re-stops with edited bytes, the O_EXCL claim succeeds afresh, a second consume row is appended, and validate_harness reports ok:true. This does not violate the four numbered D-065 obligations as written, which is why it does not by itself decide the gate; but it directly bounds two stronger claims the D-067 audit document makes and that a D-070 adjudicator would otherwise credit: section 1's 'every consume row in the ledger permanently pins the bytes it admitted', and section 2's table row 'Fabricated or post-hoc edited result | invisible | validator error, from the append-only ledger'. The pin holds only until the next consume row for that assignment. This is also the round-3 finding F-R3-10 in a later state: the reverse reconciliation closed the window between reopen and re-consume, not the window after it. I flag it separately because it is a claim-scope correction, not a bypass: a genuine rerun after --reopen legitimately produces new bytes, and the validator cannot distinguish that from a laundered edit.
assumptions_used: --reopen is a documented, supported parent operation, so exercising it is not the deliberate-forgery residual.
The .claim file is gitignored working state that no contract requires to persist.

findings.statement: Control check requested by the assignment: the D-070 ORTHOGONAL SSOT block added to validate_harness.py cannot interfere with the admission checks. It is positioned after all admission and ledger reconciliation (validate_harness.py:265-341); it only ever appends to the same `errors` list and never clears, filters, or short-circuits it, and the terminal `if errors:` at line 343 is unconditional, so it cannot mask an admission error. It shells out to check_ssot_consistency.py as a subprocess rather than importing it, and that file performs no writes (no write_text/open-for-write/unlink/mkdir anywhere in its 1478 lines), so it cannot mutate receipts, leases, or ledgers. It fails closed in every branch: OSError, non-JSON output, and exit-non-zero-with-no-reported-errors each add an error. Applicability is keyed on GATE_REGISTRY.json being present, and the obvious bypass (delete the registry to skip the check) is closed by the `git ls-files --error-unmatch` tracked-file probe at lines 282-301. The only behavioural coupling is that a synthetic fixture harness has no registry and records ssot_consistency 'not applicable', which is why the 39 hook fixtures are unaffected -- confirmed by the suite passing unchanged.
assumptions_used: grep for write primitives is a sufficient read-only check for a script that is only ever invoked as a subprocess.
reproduction: grep -n 'write_text\|open(\|dump_json\|unlink\|mkdir' .agent-harness/scripts/check_ssot_consistency.py  # no matches
